bt67yj-p153631-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for section 2, announcing the topic: whether it is ever lawful to resist authority.

bt67yj-p153631-d1e111.summary: The paragraph opens the treatment of the distinction's second question — whether authority must sometimes be resisted — by clarifying the key term: 'authority' (potestas) here does not mean any power or capacity to act whatsoever (since even resisting the devil's temptation or a pursuing robber would then count as resisting a 'power'), but specifically the power that some hold as superiors over others as subjects, such as the power of a king, magistrate, or any official over subordinates; it is this sense of potestas to which Romans 13 ('there is no power except from God') properly applies.
claims: The 'authority' at issue in the question is specifically the power of a superior over subjects (rulers, magistrates, officials), not power or capacity in the broadest sense.
Romans 13's dictum that all power is from God applies properly to this sense of authority as superiority over subjects.

bt67yj-p153631-d1e142.summary: The paragraph lays down as sound Catholic doctrine that obedience is owed by subjects to all such authority, as the Apostle (Romans 13) and many other scriptural passages teach — and this obligation of obedience extends, per Scripture, not only to good and Christian rulers but even to wicked and unbelieving princes, such as those of the early Church.
claims: Subjects owe obedience to all legitimate authority, according to sound Catholic doctrine grounded in Scripture.
This obligation extends even to wicked and unbelieving rulers, as it did for Christians under the pagan emperors of the early Church.
concepts: obedience owed even to unjust or unbelieving rulers

bt67yj-p153631-d1e165.summary: The paragraph draws a further clarifying distinction: in the question at hand, 'authority' is taken concretely, for the persons in whom authority resides, not abstractly. Taken abstractly, authority as such can never rightly be resisted, since in itself it can only be legitimate and, as the Apostle testifies, ordained by God; hence it is universally true, as the Apostle says, that 'whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God.'
claims: The question concerns authority taken concretely (as embodied in particular rulers), not abstractly.
Authority taken abstractly is by definition legitimate and divinely ordained, and can never rightly be resisted.
concepts: authority as inherently legitimate in the abstract

bt67yj-p153631-d1e187.summary: The paragraph specifies the real sense of the question — whether subjects may or must ever resist superiors, either simply by disobeying their commands or even by forcibly repelling them — and gives the first part of the answer: it is never lawful to resist superiors who use their authority rightly and lawfully, that is, as the Master says, in everything God commands them to be given; and God commands whatever is prescribed within the limits of the authority derived from him.
claims: The question concerns two possible forms of resistance: simple disobedience and forcible resistance.
It is never lawful to resist a superior who exercises authority rightly and within the God-derived limits of that authority.
concepts: limits of authority derived from God

bt67yj-p153631-d1e218.summary: The paragraph treats the case where a superior commands something beyond the proper limits of his authority: a distinction is drawn between whether the thing commanded is good, evil, or indifferent. If it is good or indifferent, the subject is not strictly bound to obey (owing to the commander's defect of authority), but is nevertheless generally bound to comply in order to avoid scandal or the appearance of disobedience — as Christ, not himself obligated, chose to pay the temple tax for himself and Peter (Matthew 17) to avoid giving offense.
claims: When a superior commands something good or indifferent but beyond his proper authority, the subject is not strictly obligated to obey, yet is usually still bound to comply to avoid scandal.
Christ's payment of the temple tax exemplifies voluntary compliance with an improperly authorized command, undertaken to avoid scandal rather than out of strict obligation.
concepts: defect of authority (excess of proper limits)
Christ's example of the temple tax

bt67yj-p153631-d1e247.summary: The paragraph treats the case where what is commanded is evil and contrary to God's law: here obedience must never be given, since such a command not only exceeds the authority of the one commanding but also subverts the order of supreme authority (God's). Peter's response to the priestly rulers who forbade preaching the Gospel ('we must obey God rather than men,' Acts 5) exemplifies this, as do the apostles and martyrs, the seven Maccabee brothers before Antiochus, and the three youths before Nebuchadnezzar who refused to worship the statue; Augustine (Sermon 6 on the Words of the Lord) is cited for the principle that a lesser authority commanding what one ought not do may rightly be despised out of fear of the greater authority, by analogy with subordinate human authorities.
claims: When authority commands something evil or contrary to God's law, obedience must never be given, because such a command subverts the order of the supreme (divine) authority.

Scriptural and patristic exempla (Peter and the apostles, the Maccabees, the three youths in Babylon, Augustine's teaching) establish and illustrate the principle that a lower authority commanding wrongdoing may and must be disregarded out of obedience to the higher authority.
concepts: scriptural and patristic exempla of righteous disobedience

bt67yj-p153631-d1e302.summary: The paragraph turns to the harder question of whether it is ever lawful actively to resist by force a superior who unjustly oppresses his subjects. This is less clear-cut, but it appears that it is sometimes lawful for the nobles and the people of an entire kingdom collectively, as shown by the history of Rehoboam (3 Kings 12) and by Augustine's words (City of God XVII.21; On the Unity of the Church, ch. 21), who does not regard as blameworthy a people's act of deposing a king bent on tyrannical rule; the reasoning given is that public authority resides in the nobles and people collectively, who can vindicate themselves from manifest tyranny, choose a legitimate prince, and even, for just cause, deprive an already-chosen ruler of his rule.
claims: It can be lawful for the collective body of a kingdom's nobles and people, but not for private individuals, to resist and even depose a tyrannical ruler.

The rationale is that public authority resides in the collective body (nobles and people), giving it the standing to vindicate itself against manifest tyranny, to choose a legitimate ruler, and to remove one already chosen for just cause.
This position is supported by the biblical precedent of Rehoboam and by Augustine's statements.
concepts: collective vs. private resistance to tyranny
public authority residing in nobles and people

bt67yj-p153631-d1e335.summary: The paragraph restricts the preceding conclusion sharply: no private individual, however, may forcibly resist a superior even if he rules tyrannically, and still less may a private person kill him, as is clear from the Decalogue's precept 'Thou shalt not kill' and from the definition of the Council of Constance (session 15, which condemned tyrannicide). David's own conduct illustrates this: though Saul was delivered into his hand, David refused to kill him himself or allow others to do so, saying 'who shall stretch out his hand against the Lord's anointed and be innocent?' (1 Kings 26) — even though David, though already anointed king, had not yet been confirmed by the people's acclamation and held no actual royal power.
claims: No private individual may forcibly resist, and still less kill, even a tyrannical superior, per the Decalogue and the Council of Constance's condemnation of tyrannicide.
David's sparing of Saul, despite having the opportunity and despite Saul's tyranny, exemplifies and confirms this prohibition on private resistance and tyrannicide.
concepts: prohibition of private resistance and tyrannicide
Council of Constance's condemnation of tyrannicide
David and Saul as scriptural exemplum

bt67yj-p153631-d1e367.summary: The chapter closes by invoking Cyprian's authority on this point: in his letter to Demetrianus defending the innocence of Christians against their slanderers, Cyprian writes that no Christian, however numerous and populous their community, resists when seized or avenges himself against unjust violence, but that the certainty of future divine vengeance makes them patient, so that the innocent yield to the guilty and the blameless submit to punishments and torments.
claims: Cyprian's testimony that Christians patiently submit to unjust violence, trusting in future divine vindication rather than resisting, is cited as confirming the doctrine of non-resistance by private individuals.
concepts: patientia grounded in trust in divine vengeance

bt67yj-p153631.summary: Capitulum 2 answers the second question of distinction 44 — whether it is ever lawful to resist authority — by first clarifying that 'authority' means rulership over subjects, owed obedience even under wicked rulers, and that abstractly considered authority can never rightly be resisted since it is inherently legitimate and divinely ordained. Taking authority concretely, in the persons who hold it, the chapter distinguishes: obedience is owed absolutely when a superior acts within his proper authority; when a superior exceeds his authority commanding something good or indifferent, strict obedience is not owed but compliance is usually still advisable to avoid scandal; when a superior commands something evil, obedience must always be refused, per scriptural and patristic exempla of righteous disobedience; the collective body of a kingdom's nobles and people may sometimes justly resist and even depose a tyrant, but no private individual may forcibly resist, and none may ever kill, even a tyrannical ruler, as confirmed by the Decalogue, the Council of Constance, David's example, and Cyprian's testimony to Christian non-resistance.
claims: Authority as such (abstractly considered) can never be resisted, being inherently legitimate and divinely ordained; the question concerns authority concretely, as held by particular rulers.
Obedience is owed absolutely to a superior acting within his proper authority.
A superior's command exceeding his authority need not be strictly obeyed if good or indifferent, though compliance to avoid scandal is usually advisable; a command to do evil must never be obeyed.

The collective body of a kingdom (nobles and people) may sometimes justly resist or depose a tyrant, but private individuals may never forcibly resist, and none may ever kill, even a tyrannical ruler.
concepts: collective vs. private resistance to tyranny
